answer.answer: The Apollo archival clips show that astronauts walked on the Moon, performed EVA fieldwork lasting from a couple of hours (Apollo 11) to many hours across later missions, and collected and returned large quantities of lunar material to Earth [6][7][5][2].  They used handheld and suit‑mounted cameras (including Hasselblad photography in lunar orbit) and crew retrieved film and other data after missions [3][2][7].  Some missions increased crew mobility so they could travel farther, leave scientific experiments and even deploy a small subsatellite, while teams on later landings emphasized geology and sampling techniques [2][7][5].  Taken together the reels show twelve astronauts on six landings conducting EVAs, returning a total of 842 pounds of rocks, core samples, pebbles, sand and dust and, on at least one mission, about 180 pounds from a more mobile sortie [5][2][6][4].  The archive also includes footage about later and different activities — for example orbital searches for hydrogen/water and contemporary plans to return with robots and humans — but those clips document subsequent science, not the Apollo surface operations themselves [1][8].

chronology.claim: Archive material notes that since the 1960s scientists suspected water (hydrogen/oxygen) could be trapped in lunar soil and later orbital instruments were designed to look for it [1].
Highlights identify Apollo 15’s increased mobility, a roughly 180‑pound sample return from that sortie, deployment of a small subsatellite, and film retrieval operations [2].
In lunar orbit, astronauts took large‑format photographs (Hasselblad) of the Moon and Earth, documenting that much imagery work was done from orbit as well as on the surface [3].
Apollo 11 footage shows the first lunar EVA (Armstrong’s first boot print and ~2.5 hours of surface time), and other 1969 clips document EVA movements and sample collection techniques [6][4][5].
Apollo 17’s geologist‑astronaut logged many more hours outside (about 22 hours across three excursions) and trained crews to do field geology with suit‑mounted cameras and backpacks [7].
Modern NASA material in the archive emphasizes that much remains to learn about the Moon and that robots and humans will continue exploration in the future [8].

answer.caveats: Several clips in the reel set are about later or non‑surface activities rather than Apollo surface work: [1] discusses orbital/remote searches for hydrogen/water (not Apollo sample returns), and [8] is a modern (2019) overview of future exploration.  Clip [3] documents photography from lunar orbit (Apollo 8) rather than surface EVA, so orbit footage is not direct evidence of surface operations.  Many of the era labels come from the footage’s video/scene metadata (e.g. [1],[2],[3],[5]) so those date markers are tied to the archive’s era tags rather than independent provenance.  The clips do not by themselves prove the presence of water on the Moon or provide comprehensive technical details (for example the archive snippets here do not show all vehicle or rover hardware), they only show the activities and sample returns recorded in these selected moments.

evidence.title: Water on the Moon
evidence.spoken: Since the 1960s, scientists have suspected that frozen water could survive in permanently shadowed craters at the Moon's poles. Both hydrogen and oxygen could be trapped within the lunar soil. So to find water on the Moon, scientists are looking for indications of hydrogen using the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's LEND neutron Detector. By observing the interaction of neutrons with the lunar soil, scientists can interpret how much hydrogen is likely to be present. In order to make a detailed interpretation, however, LEND needs to observe a large number of neutrons.
